en: The commentary on the *Sādhana* titled *Samantabhadra*, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) called *Ādiyoga*: "Nor is there nirvāṇa in non-existence; how much less could there be existence for this?"
"The exhaustion of the grasping at existence and non-existence is called nirvana," as stated by the Blessed One.
It has been said: "Indeed, non-nirvāṇa is taught as nirvāṇa by the Lord of the World;
it is like that which is made by space."
"The knot has been released by space itself.
Thus, to this extent is the first limb called service (sevā).
That which is called a deity, resembling its cause, is said to be the soft outflow fruit. (50)
He states the second limb:
"Thereafter" means immediately following the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). "By the radiance of their own seed-syllables" refers to the six [bodhisattvas] beginning with Kṣitigarbha.

By means of the seed-syllables, beginning with *kṣīṃ* and so forth, located respectively in the positions of the eyes and other sense organs, residing within the pericarp of their respective insignia.

The meaning is: "by their very lights" and "by those very [deities] possessing light. Thus, those such as Kṣitigarbha and others who are produced by the causes that are the lights of their own respective seeds—
The connection with what follows is: "one should meditate, having filled the six [locations] beginning with the eyes with those [syllables].
"According to their respective [places]" means in the location of the eyes and so forth.
Kṣitigarbha, born from the radiant syllable Kṣiṃ situated upon the moon within the center of a moon-disc,
[should be placed] in the locations of the ears and so forth.
The meaning is that one should visualize Vajrapāṇi and the others according to the prescribed ritual;
by this, the limb known as the "subsidiary practice" (*upasādhana*), characterized by omniscience, is attained. (52) It is [of] the soft [degree].
The fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) has been explained.
The purity of the eyes and so forth [is known] through the specific qualities such as subtlety regarding their respective objects.
Because thorough knowledge is possible.
With the words "amale" and so forth, he states the third limb. [Amale...]
The meaning is that one should meditate on the Mind-Vajra as the syllable *hūṃ* situated in the center of the hub of a vajra within the moon at one's own heart.
(54) [One should place] *ye* and *kam* respectively upon the mouth and the head, which are the lotus and the wheel.
In his navel, at the central part, is the Speech-Vajra by means of the syllable ĀḤ;
the Praṇava is the syllable OṂ, and by that one should meditate upon the Body-Vajra— such is the connection.
The "hearts" of those [deities] such as Cittavajra and the others; [these are] masses of light rays. For here, within their hearts—
The syllables HŪṂ, ĀḤ, and OṂ, situated respectively upon a moon, a vajra, and a lotus wheel, are to be visualized;
the meaning is that they consist of masses of light rays. (56)
By those forms of the offering goddesses, such as Rūpavajrā, which emerge from the tips of the rays shining through contact with true wisdom,
[they fill] all around the ten directions.
Having worshipped the Lords of Jinas who are established there, and being honored by those very Lords of Jinas—
who shine through association with the truly wise—
"Subsequently" means that one should consecrate the Mind-Vajra and the others in the sequence beginning with "the glorious holder of the Mind-Vajra.
[The verse continues: "The glorious holder of the Mind-Vajra is the embodiment of the indivisibility of the three vajras."
May the Vajra-Mind today perform the rite of empowerment for me. ||58||
"Those who meditate on the indivisibility of the three vajras" means that the three vajras— the body-vajra and so forth—
are meditated upon as indivisible; their intrinsic nature is that [of the indivisible].
This is the meaning:
"May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are conceived as the indivisibility of the three vajras and who arise from the mind, grant me the state of empowerment this very day. (59)
(= Guhyasamāja XII.75) (58) Oṃ! I am of the nature of the vajra-mind of all Tathāgatas;
the glorious Dharma is indeed the path of speech.
Meditated upon as the indivisible nature of the three vajras,
may he today bestow upon me the state of empowerment of the Vajra of Speech.
(= Guhyasamāja XII,72) Dharma is the speech-vajra (*vāgvajra*);
"the path of speech" (*vākpatha*) refers to that which is established as speech. As for the remainder...
This is indeed well known:
"May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are meditated upon as the indivisibility of the three vajras,
grant him the state of empowerment."
Arising from the path of speech. ||61||
(= Guhyasamāja XII.73) Oṃ! I am of the nature of the speech-vajra of all Tathāgatas;
I am the glorious bearer of the Buddha-body, meditated upon as the indivisibility of the three vajras.
May the Vajra-Body today bestow upon me the state of empowerment. ||62||
(= Guhyasamāja XII,70) May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who have meditated upon the indivisibility of the three vajras,
grant me today the state of empowerment characterized by the [three] bodies. 63.
(= Guhyasamāja XII,71) (60) Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-body of all Tathāgatas; then, of this triple-vajra which has been empowered by these verses and mantras...
He says this in order to explain its nature as purity.
"Like the sky," and so forth.
Precisely because it is free from the characteristics of the apprehended object and so on, emptiness has a nature like the sky.
The meaning is that this form is to be seen as the three vajras.
Thus,
having perceived this pure form of the three vajras, one should have a crown resplendent with the [deity] born of one's own family.
The connection [with the subsequent] follows later;
however, by this much, the member called the "proof" (sādhana) is established.
The fruit of human effort characterized by the soft [degree] is said to be the purification of the three bodies (kāya) characterized as the Dharma-body, the Enjoyment-body, and the Emanation-body.
Because the mind-vajra and the others are, respectively, the nature of the Dharma-body and so forth. (62)
He stated the fourth limb,
beginning with "having exhorted," and so forth. Here,
indeed, at the time of the accomplishment of the Mind-Vajra and the others:
Thus, in the space between the mind-vajra and the speech-vajra, the Lord Jñānasattva, appearing in the form of the Samayasattva,
is seated upon a moon disk located in the center of a sword-grip resting on a moon disk.
The entire assembly of all directions, containing the multitudes of sages dwelling within the circle of the sky, should be beheld by the splendors of his heart.
Having exhorted the assembly of Sugatas who were present, from the rays of those exalted Munis...
By those hands of the hosts of vidyās who have emerged, such as Rūpavajrā and the others,
the jars filled with gnosis were uplifted; by means of those jars, [the water of] gnosis...
Having been consecrated,
the practitioner of the Mañjuvajra-self-yoga should possess a crown shining with his own family deity.
His own family lord is Akṣobhya; by him his crown should be inflamed immediately after the consecration.
The meaning is that Akṣobhya is to be visualized upon the crown of Mañjuśrī; by means of this,
the limb of the great accomplishment (mahāsādhana) is the consecration (abhiṣeka).
The fruit of the softness and purity of form has been described; for through the consecration of the water of gnosis, one is struck down for the sake of attaining purity. That...

Thus, the four limbs beginning with service (*sevā*) are qualified by the term "inferior" because they pertain to the principal deity and are therefore not skillful, lacking the capacity to eliminate all adverse factors.
The soft [faculties] have been described as being endowed with their respective fruits. Now, four others are mentioned, beginning with the outflow (*niṣyanda*) and so forth.
These are the purifiers of wisdom. Because they occupy a middle position between the weak and the intense among the four factors,
he states the specific qualification of the term "middling."
"In that same way" means: having perceived the vidyā through the sequence of service (*sevā*) and so forth, just as with Mañjuvajra.

The connection is as follows: the mantra-knower, through the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) "I delight the Sugatas," should begin the enjoyment with her. He distinguishes the *vidyā* while demonstrating those very [acts] beginning with service (*sevā*).
"Created by the seed-syllable of Mañjuvajra at one's own heart" means [created] as the radiance of one's own deity;
that is, in the form of Mañjuvajra.
These are to be assigned as services; they are indicated as having the fruit of the intermediate outflow. (68)
Regarding the phrase "having eyes and so forth fully perfected":
in that very same way, the eyes and so forth are brought to completion by Kṣitigarbha and the others, who have arisen from their own respective seed-syllables.
The three-syllable mantra *hūṃ āḥ oṃ* is indicated as the intermediate ripened fruit, accomplished through the sixfold desire.
The meditation and placement of these [deities] in the previously mentioned locations in the form of the former deities, the mind-vajra, and so forth—
by this, the practice is indicated as having the fruit of human effort as its intermediate result.

Immediately after that, she whose radiant and stainless body has been consecrated by the water of primordial wisdom (*pūrvadeva-jñānodaka-abhiṣeka*) and other rites is "she whose body is radiant through the arrangement of syllables" (*akṣaravinyāsabhāsvaraśarīrā*).
By this, the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*) whose fruit is the purity of the middle state is indicated.
He further characterizes that very [accomplishment] as being the "peacock-feathered one" (*kalāpinī*) of the five families.
In the head, the heart,
the navel, the secret place,
and in the pair of thighs and so forth.
In due order, those which are produced by these seed-syllables— *oṃ*, *hūṃ*, *svā*, *āḥ*, and *hā*— namely,
the families beginning with the Body-Vajra and Mind-Vajra, take the form of the Body-Vajra.
The noble family is the Tathāgata family;
likewise, the mind-vajra noble family is the Vajra family.
From the word "original" (*ādya*), [the other families are understood].
The *tnakula*,
the *padmakula*, and the *karmakula* are included.
(72) Her limbs are consecrated by these five in their respective order.
"Pervading the three worlds with a circle of true radiance" means:
possessing a mass of rays shining forth that pervades the triple realm. Āḥ!
And by the syllable *kāra*, the variegated pericarp is fashioned; and by the syllable *hūṃ*,
the eight-petaled lotus is emanated.
She who is thus described is referred to as such.
(74) Having beheld her— who is of the nature of the essence of the vajra of the passion of all Tathāgatas— what kind of being did he become as he began the act of delight?
Thus he said.
The wisdom of the True One is the cause that gives birth;
it is the wisdom of Vajradhara,
whose intrinsic nature is its natural outflow (*niṣyanda*).
That minister whose own body serves as the means (upāya) is described as such;
the vajra is to be produced by the minister through the syllable *hūṃ*.
For this very reason, he will say immediately thereafter: "Hūṃ! Stainless, emerged from the vajra."
He states the mantra that is the basis for the yoga of passion:
*Oṃ*,
etc.
By this much of the text, the first [samādhi] named Ādiyoga has been explained.
Now, the other four, beginning with Sevāniṣyanda, are presented because they pertain to all the deities.

In order to express the distinctions of the words "intense" (*adhimātra*) and so forth by means of specific cognitions regarding the generalities, he describes the *maṇḍalarājāgrī* samādhi through the generation stage (*utpattikrama*),
beginning with "In the moon at the heart," and so on. (78)
The mantra located on the moon within the fist, which is situated upon the moon at the heart of the Jñānasattva,
is the "heart-moon-mantra";
by its radiance, [it purifies] all Buddhas without exception.
Having drawn the *sandoha* into one's own body through the mouth,
[one should contemplate it] in the form of all one's own *māṇḍaleyas*.
The connection is as follows: having meditated upon [the deity] produced from his own heart, one of steady mind, for the sake of the welfare of the world, should emit [the seed-syllable].
By means of the syllable *hūṃ*, the *vajra*— the *hūṃ-vajra*— emerges through that path; being stainless and having the form of an excellent mind,
it is introduced [into the heart] as that which is born from the transformation of the assembly of Buddhas.
Regarding "bodhicitta": having visualized it as residing within the lotus-like womb of the Goddess, like a bee within a lotus. (80)
"Born from one's own heart" means that one's own heart is the syllable *maṃ* as previously described;
through the process of its transformation, it takes on the form of all the deities of one's own maṇḍala.
Having meditated upon that very *bodhicitta* thus arisen in this manner,
the yogi should, according to the method to be described, emit it from the interior of the goddess’s lotus in order to establish the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) within the maṇḍala.
The meaning is that one should emit [it].
As it has been said: "First is emptiness, enlightenment is second."

The collection of seeds is the third, the manifestation of the image is the fourth, and the placement of the syllables is the fifth. He now describes that very procedure for the emission of the wheel of deities arisen from the lotus: (82)
"Having exhorted," and so forth. The Mind-Vajra is Akṣobhya as previously described, endowed with specific qualities.
"Endowed with arms like those of the Primordial Supreme One" means with arms like those of Vajrasattva, holding a vajra, sword, lotus, and jewel.
Endowed with this, having been exhorted by the emission mantra *vajradhṛk*, it is to be withdrawn; thus is the detailed exposition on the radiation and so forth.

Having brought [the object] by withdrawing its forms, the wise one should, with his entire being and whole self, cause Mañjuśrī to enter into his own form; thus, he is free from the grasping of both the object of entry and the agent of entry. (84)
The body-vajra is Vairocana, characterized by the aforementioned attributes and the symbols of the wheel and so forth— namely,
the wheel, sword, lotus, and jewel.
It is marked;
likewise, with the *utsarga* mantra "cittavajra vajra jinajik."
Having exhorted [the disciple], one should meditate [on the deity] in the center of the moon within a lotus;
[visualizing him] as having a youthful appearance with faces on the right, left, and middle.
O Mañjuśrī, [the six arms] are blue, white, and yellow, resembling refined gold, with six beautiful hands adorned with emeralds and other gems.
Ratneśa, whose complexion is like radiant gold, adorned with six hands beautified by an emerald, a lotus, a sword, a wheel, and the embrace of Prajñā.
The connection is that, having exhorted [the practitioner] with "Ratnasaṃbhava, holder of jewels," one should meditate [on him] to the right of Mañjuvajra. (88)
"Red as the hue of a lotus" means as crimson as a ruby (*padmarāga*).
"The two faces are like that" means that his face, too, is like that of Kumāra.
In the description of the right and left [hands], they are blue and white,
with hands bearing marks such as lotuses and so forth.
Having exhorted [the disciple] with the words, "O Āro[li], [visualize] Amitābha, of blazing radiance, his hands distinguished by a red lotus, a sword, a wheel, and a jewel."
The meaning is that one should meditate [on him] to the west of Mañjuvajra.
"Having the luster of an emerald" means having a color similar to a green gem.
"Endowed with a face and other features as before."
He is endowed with the excellence of the blue and white faces on the right and left, the radiation of various kinds of light rays, and so forth, as previously described;
[he is] equipped with the sword and other [implements].
Thus:
endowed with a sword, a wheel, a lotus, and a jewel— Amoghasiddhi.
The meaning is that, having exhorted him with "O you who possess wisdom," one should meditate upon [him] to the north of Mañjuvajra. (92)
He states the common qualifiers for all of them: "rucira... and so forth; [they are] those with beautiful matted hair and crowns.
And they are so described because they are radiant with the splendor of supreme pride and possess blazing ornaments. "With bodies presided over by knowledge" means embraced—
"All [deities] have their own respective wisdom-consorts," meaning that those other than Vairocana are to be meditated upon within a solar mandala;
for it has been stated that Vairocana is seated upon a lunar throne. (94)

"O you who possess the luster of the Body-Vajra of the erotic sentiment! O Locanā-devī, endowed with the erotic rasa through your face and other features, resembling Vairocana, seated upon the full moon, and of supreme, pure form!"
The meaning is that by means of the mantra "moharati," through exhortation, she should be visualized there in the northeastern direction by means of meditative concentration (dhyāna).

"Regarding 'nairṛtī' and so forth: Māmakī, who is intensely eager for great austerity and possesses the form described above, being exhorted as 'one who delights in hatred,' [is situated] in the southwest corner."
The meaning is "should be seen.
Amitābha [resides] in the stainless body of Vāgīśā.
Van is she whose body has a stainless complexion and so forth, known as Pāṇḍarā,
possessing the form as described, who is called Rāgarati; thus impelled, she resides in the direction of the wind.
He should be visualized as Ratnasambhava, possessing a beautiful form,
color, and other qualities like those of the Lord of Jewels.
Sadṛkṣatārā, with the aforementioned attributes,
urged forth as Vajrarati,
is to be visualized in the northeastern direction.
He states the primary characteristics of these [perfections].
Regarding "saccakre" and so forth: "the remaining ones" refers to Locanā; [these are] the sword, the lotus, and the jewel.
The remaining signs are thus those of Māmakī.
For Pāṇḍarā, there are a sword, a wheel, and a jewel; for Tārā, the meaning is a sword, a lotus, and a jewel. (100)
"In the maṇḍala," and so forth; [this refers to] the four corners beginning with the southeast,
and on both sides of the main entrance.
The six goddesses, beginning with Rūpavajrā, resemble the Body-Vajra and the others respectively; they abide within these three realities.

Having emitted [the seed-syllables] with the mantra "oṃ āḥ hūṃ," one should meditate upon the primary symbols, such as the mirror and so forth, according to the ritual procedure to be described hereafter. This is the meaning.
In that context, the body is Vairocana—
Canas is marked with a mirror;
Rūpavajrā is marked with a sword, a lotus, and the remaining jewel-mark. (102)
Śabdavajrā resembles Cittavajra; her emblem is a lute, and she possesses the remaining emblems of a sword, a lotus, and a jewel. Gandhavajrā resembles Ratneśa; her emblem is a scent-conch.
[She also possesses] a sword, a lotus, and a wheel.
And marked with the remaining signs;
she is Rasavajrā, resembling Vāgvajrā, and filled with the vessel of delicious tastes.
She is marked by the lotus-vessel;
she is also marked by the remaining symbols of the sword, the wheel, and the jewel.
She is Sparśavajrā, the Unfailing One.
Dharmadhātuvajrā resembles Vajrasattva; her garments and insignia are like those [of the other goddesses], and she possesses the remaining insignia of the sword, lotus, and jewel.
She is marked with the symbol of the dharmodaya-mudrā,
and possesses the remaining symbols of the sword, lotus, and jewel.
Regarding the phrase "of the full moon mandala," it was stated previously as well.
This should be applied to all the goddesses. (104) Now he speaks of the wrathful gatekeepers,
beginning with "at the eastern gate," and so forth.
He whose light is infinite and formidable, pervading all directions, is called Sarvāśāvarty-anantabhīmābha.
"Having the appearance of a mass of fierce clouds at the time of dissolution" means having the form of a dense collection of fierce clouds at the time of the end of the world.
The king of the mind is Akṣobhya; equal to him by way of arms, faces, and so forth is that body which is the form of Yamāri. (106)
He was distinguished by the radiance of many fierce families of deities who had issued forth from him;
thus, cruel serpents served as his bodily ornaments.
Adorned with the limbs of fierce serpents,
he is glorious and endowed with all accomplishments.
Being thus described as "the son of Vivasvat," "the end-maker," "Yamāntaka," and "the one who makes an end of Yama," he,
being thus exhorted, [appears] within the radiant solar disc (*sūryamaṇḍala*).
He set out for the one renowned as being at the eastern gate; that is to say, he went there to see him. (108)
"South," and so forth.
Because he dispels the darkness of the world, he is the unsurpassed light, the Lord of the Body (kāyeśa).
Vairocana is likewise fierce by virtue of his arms, faces, and colors;
being thus constituted, he is unassailable by the Māras, such as the afflictions (kleśa).
Being thus exhorted as "the Unconquered," "the Overpowering," "the One of Fierce Form," and "the Maker of the End of Ignorance," [he acted].
He who stands at the southern gate should be visualized as Bhāsvatī.
(110) [The deity] Hayakandhara and the others are like Vāgvajra in their arms and other features.
Thus, with the colors of his arms and faces resembling Amitābha,
Hayagrīva is described according to the remaining specifications as stated.
The concise meaning is that, having been thus exhorted as "Padmāntakṛt," he is to be visualized at the western gate within a radiant maṇḍala. (112)
He states the emanation of Vighnāntaka with the words "like Akṣobhya" and so forth;
he is similar to Akṣobhya in terms of his arms, faces, and colors.
The Noble One, fierce like the fire at the time of universal dissolution, is an ocean of nectar; he who is far removed from unwholesome states through his meritorious qualities.
He is noble because of his transcendence;
he is a hero because he has destroyed all obstacles.
The meaning is that, having been thus exhorted as "Vighnāntakṛt," he should be meditated upon situated within a sun-maṇḍala at the northern gate. (114)
"Vairocana," and so forth.
Immediately after the consecration of these very deities, Yamāri and the others, [the syllables] appear upon their crowns.
They should be visualized in succession as Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi.
The four primary symbols, beginning with the mallet, should be visualized in the hand in their proper sequence; by the word "beginning" (ādi), [other implements are implied].
The meaning is that even the sword and other such weapons should be applied according to the circumstances;
for although they take the form of wrath, their sole purpose is the disciplining of sentient beings by those who are compassionate.
Thus it is said in the *Mahāsamayatattva*: "Aho!
How truly firm is the great Vajra-activity of all the Buddhas, which is peaceful..."
"Even those who are fierce become fierce for the sake of benefiting others.
Likewise, in the *Guhyatilaka*: "Aho!"...
For indeed, the knowledge of mastery belongs to the Buddhas who perceive reality; for therein, the pure means and disciplines attain the state of wrath, and so forth. (116)
"Thus, on all sides," and so forth;
"thus" means by the sequence just mentioned;
"on all sides" (*paritaḥ*) means in every way.
Having beheld the completed maṇḍala with one's whole being,
[one should visualize] the rays of light from the mantra at the heart of the Jñānasattva as hooks; by these, [the deities] are summoned.
One should visualize the Sugatas, drawn forth and appearing in the form of a mandala-circle, standing before the samaya-maṇḍala; by this,
the jñāna-maṇḍala—
Plowing has been explained.
(118) "Wisdom," and so forth:
wisdom is the female form, and means (*upāya*) is [the male form].
That which is this stainless samādhi, consisting of the male form, composed of wisdom and skillful means, and having the nature of wisdom and skillful means— from that, there arises true bliss.
By him that wheel was filled; "by Antaka,
Mathana, and the others" means by Yamāntaka and the rest,
who performed the protection.
The yogin should meditate thus;
and this should also be understood in the context of the *samayamaṇḍala*.
"From one's own heart" means consecrated by one's own seed-syllable (*bīja*), such as sandalwood...

Having offered worship with flowers and other offerings to that maṇḍala-cakra, one should [dissolve] that maṇḍala-cakra according to its own nature through the sequence of summoning, entering, binding, and pleasing, beginning with Yamāntaka and the others.
Having internalized that very same perfected mandala-circle within the samaya-mandala, like oil within sand; thus [it is].
"Like one who has performed his own consecration" means like Mañjuvajra,
having received consecration through the sequence of service (*sevā*) and so forth, according to the procedure to be described hereafter.
Being self-restrained, one should worship— that is, honor—
the sequence of the manifestation of the deities of the mandala therein; that is the superior common service.
It is the fruit of outflow.
(122) That which, as previously stated, is the basis for the eye and so forth,
is the superior purification of the general [faculties].
The fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*):
that which, as previously stated, is the basis of mind and so forth,
is the common possession (*sāmānyasādhana*).
The fruit of superior human effort (*adhimātra-puruṣakāra-phala*) is as follows:
that sequence of consecration by the water of gnosis (*jñāna-ambu-abhiṣeka-krama*),
which is the common (*sāmānya*) *mahāsādhana*, is the fruit of superior purity (*vaimalya*).
And immediately after the consecration,
Akṣobhya is to be visualized upon the crown of the Tathāgatas Vairocana and the others; likewise,
Vairocana [is to be visualized] upon Locanā and Rūpavajrā.
For Māmakī, Śabdavajrā, and Dharmadhātuvajrā, Akṣobhya is the presiding deity;
for Pāṇḍarā and Rasavajrā, Amitābha is the presiding deity.
Amoghasiddhi [is the lord] of Tārā and Sparśavajrā;
Gandhavajrā [is the consort].
Ratnasambhava is she;
these alone are declared to be the presiding deities of Yamāri and the others. (124)

Thus, he explains by means of the six noble verses beginning with "In the interior of the lotus" (*kamalodare*) and ending with "worship" (*pūjā*), the ritual procedure by which the wheel (*cakra*)— into which the consecration has been infused— is to be worshipped.
By means of the light from the seed-syllable at the heart of the Jñānasattva,
having drawn in all [beings] beginning with those of various forms,
and having caused them to enter one's own body and emerge through the path of the vajra—
One should meditate on the circle of rays, which is the very nature of the *bodhicitta*, within the interior of the lotus of the *vidyā*.
(126) "From this" means having thus meditated upon that very [form], which is the counterpart of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Arising from his body hair,
it was an array of various kinds of light rays,
spreading out and pervading the entire expanse of space.
Being "wise" (matimān), which means being free from the perception of duality,
one should emit [the light] everywhere, in every way; then, by means of the rays emerging from the mouth...
"Adorned with all ornaments of pure crystal" refers to the goddesses of form and so forth;
"in sequence" means respectively by means of the six symbols, such as the mirror and the rest.
And she shines, resplendent with her playful sprout-like hands, through the radiance of her splendor, appearing as if adorned with swords, lotuses, and other such implements as appropriate.
And from those [lotuses], with their radiant limbs and trunks,
there issued forth a spreading web of various offerings.

The spreading forth of clouds of offerings such as forms and so on; by means of those [offerings], there is the analytical knowledge (*pratisamvid*) of things in their illusory-like nature and other such aspects.
And that which is worldly view, consisting of the cultivation of dance, song, and so forth, which are in accordance with the world and attached to its objects— by means of those two,
through wholesome [practices]...
By means of those [deities] who have become the cause for the arising of non-conceptual great bliss:
(132) *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of worship of all Tathāgatas.* Likewise, by means of the goddesses such as Rūpavajrā who are of such a nature...

And with all external perfumes and so forth, [he worships] the Lords of Jinas situated within the mandala-circle: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the worship of all Tathāgatas. Thus [he says].

By means of the mantra of the empowerment of worship, the yogi—freed from the conceptual construction of distinctions between the object of worship, the worshiper, and the act of worship—should perform the worship. (134)
Now he speaks of the offering of praise,
beginning with "pratiśabda" and so forth;
following that [is the word] "tadanu."
Immediately following the ritual of worship, he articulated the entire collection of words in the form of praise, like an echo.
Within one's own mind, one should perceive the presiding deity as the principal deity; through the praise of that [deity], there is happiness.
O Akṣobhyavajra, great wisdom, Vajradhātu,
great Buddha; O Trimaṇḍala, supreme among the three vajras, Vajraghoṣa, homage be to you!
(= Guhyasamāja XVII,1) [.....
a]kṣobhyaḥ | He himself, because of his indivisibility, is the vajra, the perfectly pure dharmadhātu—
Because his nature is gnosis, he is the Great Gnosis (*mahājñāna*).
He is indivisible.
Because he is the source of the [vajra] elements, he is the Vajra Realm (*vajradhātu*).
He is the Great Sage (*mahābudha*).
He is the "Three Mandalas" because he consists of the mandalas of body, speech, and mind.
[He resides] within the vajras of the body and so forth.
Because the mind is primary, he is the foremost of the three vajras;
and such is Akṣobhya at every step.
Having awakened, "Homage be to you"—they spoke these words of praise to you through the gateways of the Dharma:
"O Sound," they said; "O Vajra."
The meaning is: "the state of non-dual reality.
O Vairocana, Greatly Pure One, Peaceful Vajra, Great Joy;
teach the phenomena that are luminous by nature, O Vajra; homage be to you!
(= Guhyasamāja XVII,2) (138) Thus, from Virocana comes Vairocana;
[he is] for the sake of sentient beings free from afflictions.
Because he possesses sovereignty over the great, pure, indivisible, and peaceful activity (*śāntika*), he is Vajraśānta;
because his nature is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).
The Great Joy is supreme among those whose nature is luminous by virtue of its being the essence of mirror-like wisdom;
having thus awakened them, he taught.
"O Vajra, homage be to you! they said as before.
"O King of Jewels, most profound, Vajra of Space, stainless as the sky, pure by nature, untainted—homage be to you, O Vajra Body."
(= Guhyasamāja XVII,3) "In the King of Jewels" refers to Ratnasambhava,
because of his profound depth.
Extremely profound; because it is indivisible like space due to its vajra-nature, it is the Space-Vajra (khavajra);
because it is the gnosis of equality...
It is as stainless as space; it is that very same naturally pure [nature],
untainted due to the removal of the stains of afflictions, karma, birth, and the latencies of the knowable.
"...Like space... [Body-Vajra], homage be to you! they said as before.
(140) "O Great King Vajrāmṛta, free from conceptual construction, wielder of the space-vajra;
O Vajra of Speech who has attained the perfection of passion, homage be to you!"
(= Guhyasamāja XVII,4) "Vajrāmṛta" refers to Amitābha...
